      CASE NO: 25VECV06434 

 

[TENTATIVE] RULING RE: DEFENDANT’S MOTIONS TO COMPEL PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSES TO INITIAL DISCOVERY 

 

Dept. U 

8:30 a.m. 

August 12, 2026 

 

  1. BACKGROUND 

This case is a slip and fall action filed by Plaintiff Verania Aguilar against Defendant In-N-Out Burgers. 

On November 10, 2025, Plaintiff filed her complaint against Defendant. 

On December 31, 2025, Defendant filed its answer to the complaint. 

On February 13, 2026, Defendant served Plaintiff with requests for production of documents (the “RFPs”), form interrogatories (the “FROGs”), and special interrogatories (the “SROGs”).  Despite Defendant’s subsequent efforts to meet and confer, Plaintiff failed to timely respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs.  (Cenac decl., ¶¶ 3-5.) 

On May 13, 2026, Defendant filed its motions to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs. 

On July 29, 2026, and on August 5, 2026, Defendant filed its notices of Plaintiff’s non-opposition to the motions. 

As of 9:00 A.M. on August 7, 2026, Plaintiff had filed no opposition brief. 

  1. RULING 

The motions are granted.  Defendant is awarded sanctions against Plaintiff in the total amount of $1,980.00. 

  1. LEGAL STANDARD  

  1. Motion to Compel Initial Responses to Requests for Production of Documents 

Where there has been no response to a demand to produce documents, the demanding party may seek an order compelling a response.¿ Code Civ. Proc., § 2031.300. 

  1. Motion to Compel Initial Responses to Interrogatories  

If a party to whom interrogatories are directed fails to serve a timely response, the demanding party may move for an order compelling a response.¿ Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.290. 

  1. DISCUSSION 

Defendant moves to compel Plaintiff’s initial responses to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs. 

On February 13, 2026, Defendant served the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs on Plaintiff.  Despite Defendant’s efforts to meet and confer, Plaintiff failed to timely respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs.  Defendant is entitled to an order compelling Plaintiff to respond to the RFPs, the FROGs, and the SROGs, without stating objections, within thirty (30) days.  See Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2030.290, 2031.300. 

The trial court shall impose a monetary sanction when granting a motion to compel initial responses to a request for production of documents or interrogatories, unless the court finds circumstances would make the imposition a sanction unjust.¿ Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2030.290 (c), 2031.300 (c). 

Defendant has been waiting on Plaintiff’s responses to basic discovery for several months.  Despite Defendant’s efforts to meet and confer, Plaintiff failed to provide initial responses.  Defendant is entitled to recover its attorneys’ fees. 

The Court calculates reasonable attorneys’ fees under the lodestar.¿ See PLCM Group v. Drexler (2000) 22 Cal.4th 1084, 1096. 

As to each motion, Defendant requests $2,910.00, representing 9.5 hours of attorney time at $300.00/hour, plus the motion’s $60.00 filing fee.  Defendant’s request is reasonable as to counsel’s $300.00/hour rate but inflated as to the number of hours billed.  5.0 hours is a reasonable total amount of time for counsel to have spent preparing all three (3) motions, which are largely duplicative.  Plaintiff filed no opposition brief(s), and Defendant filed no reply.  The lodestar will be adjusted accordingly.  Defendant may recover 1.0 additional hour of attorney time for counsel to appear at the hearing on all three (3) motions.¿ Defendant may also recover each motion’s $60.00 filing fee. 

In sum, Defendant will be awarded its attorneys’ fees against Plaintiff in the total amount of $1,980.00.¿ (6.0 hours x $300.00/hour + $60.00 filing fee x 3 = $1,980.00.) 

The Court notes that Defendant has separately filed a motion to deem Plaintiff’s responses to requests for admission admitted.  Plaintiff is strongly encouraged to work with Defendant to informally resolve outstanding discovery issues before the hearing on that motion on October 20, 2026. 

  1. CONCLUSION  

Plaintiff Verania Aguilar is ORDERED to provide initial responses to Defendant In-N-Out Burgers’s Requests for Production of Documents, Form Interrogatories, and Special Interrogatories, without stating objections, within thirty (30) days of this order. 

 

Defendant In-N-Out Burgers is AWARDED sanctions against Plaintiff Verania Aguilar 9in the total amount of $1,980.00. 

 

Defendant In-N-Out Burgers is ORDERED to give notice. 

 

DATED: August 12, 2026

Judge of the Superior Court

      CASE NO: 26STCV08352 

 

[TENTATIVE] RULING RE: PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO VACATE PROCEEDINGS AND DISMISS ACTION FOR IMPROPER VENUE, LACK OF JURISDICTION, AND IRREGULARITY 

 

Dept. U 

8:30 a.m. 

August 12, 2026 

 

  1. BACKGROUND 

This case is a landlord-tenant action filed by Plaintiff Shahrooz Bigonah against Defendant “Jayeshkumar Jaykrishna and Insurance.”  Plaintiff is self-represented.1 

On March 16, 2026, Plaintiff filed his complaint against Defendant. 

On April 15, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion to vacate the proceedings and dismiss the action for improper venue, lack of jurisdiction, and irregularity. 

As of 10:00 A.M. on August 7, 2026, nothing further had been filed in this matter by any party. 

  1. RULING 

The motion is tentatively granted.  At the hearing, the Court will welcome Plaintiff’s clarification as to the intent of his motion. 

  1. LEGAL STANDARD 

An action may be dismissed, “[w]ith or without prejudice, upon written request of the plaintiff to the clerk, filed with papers in the case, or by oral or written request to the court at any time before the actual commencement of trial, upon payment of the costs, if any.”  Code Civ. Proc., § 581 (b)(1). 

  1. DISCUSSION 

Plaintiff moves to vacate the proceedings and dismiss the action for improper venue, lack of jurisdiction, and irregularity. 

If Plaintiff truly intends to dismiss his complaint, Plaintiff may do so.  See Code Civ. Proc., § 581 (b)(1).  The Court is, however, concerned by irregularities in Plaintiff’s motion that make it unclear whether Plaintiff truly intends to dismiss this action. 

Plaintiff’s own motion complains that Plaintiff’s filing of the action in this Court “reflects either gross negligence or intentional forum shopping.”  (Motion, p. 2:19-21.)  Plaintiff’s own motion states that “Plaintiff knew or should have known that this case did not belong in” this Court.  (Motion, p. 3:24-26.)  Plaintiff’s own motion continues, “Defendant respectfully requests that the Court…”  (Motion, p. 4:19-20.)  The motion thus seems to indicate that Plaintiff believes he is a defendant in this case.  He is not. 

Other irregularities include that the caption page on Plaintiff’s motion lists Defendant Avalon Bay Woodland Hills, which is not a defendant named in the complaint.  Finally, the end of Plaintiff’s motion references case #26STCV09219, which does not match the case number assigned to this case (#26STCV08352). 

If Plaintiff truly intends to dismiss this case, his motion is granted.  Given irregularities in Plaintiff’s motion, however, the Court welcomes Plaintiff’s clarification as to the intent of his motion at the hearing thereon. 

  1. CONCLUSION 

Plaintiff Shahrooz Bigonah’s motion to dismiss his complaint is GRANTED. 

 

The Clerk is ORDERED to give notice. 

 

DATED: August 12, 2026

Lee S. Arian 

Judge of the Superior Court
